1.pericope_label: And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots... And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him

schools.summary: Delitzsch states the movement of the opening as a law rather than a picture: in the humble beginning lies a power that will carry it to a great height by a steady process, the twig becoming a tree with a crown laden with fruit, so that humiliation is followed by exaltation; on the second verse he reads a formal act, the Lord acknowledging the branch and consecrating and equipping him for his great work with the seven spirits. Ellicott hears the phrase about the Spirit looking both ways at once, since it was the spirit of the Lord that made men heroes and judges of old and the same spirit descending on Jesus by which men were taught to see the token that he was the Christ of God; but what is promised here is more than the heroic daring of a Jephthah or a Samson, the future king being a David and a Solomon in one.

Gill reports that a Jewish commentator took the rod for Hezekiah and dismisses that on chronology, since he was already ten or twelve years old when the words were spoken, adding that many Jewish writers ancient and modern own the Messiah here; he takes the resting of the Spirit as proof that the kingdom is spiritual and finds in the verse a clear proof of the trinity of Persons, the Spirit being one Jehovah with the Father yet distinct from him and from the Son. Calvin explains why the chapter turns where it does, since the calamities described might have terrified the godly into despair; he keeps the figure with which the previous chapter closed, Jerusalem consumed as by a single conflagration, rejects the Hezekiah reading on the ground that at his birth the house of David still had a flourishing reputation, and insists that with the second verse the prophet begins to speak of Christ plainly.

Clarke states the movement of the whole chapter as its argument, a slender twig from the root of an old withered stem, weak at first and yet to become fruitful and mighty. Wesley presses the noun for the stem, which means a trunk cut off from the root, so the Messiah was to be born of the royal house in a most forlorn condition; he draws out that the prophet says of Jesse and not of David, a private and mean person, to intimate that at Christ's birth the royal family would be reduced to its primitive obscurity; and he says it is not needful to distinguish the first two of the Spirit's gifts exactly, since it is enough that they are the qualifications of a governor and a teacher, while separating counsel as prudence to give advice from might as courage to execute it and defining the closing fear as a fear of reverence.
Henry adds a philological note, that some have thought the word for the branch here referred to in the evangelist's remark that the Messiah should be called a Nazarene.

debates.question: Is the rod out of Jesse's stem Hezekiah or the Messiah?

positions.view: The Messiah; the Hezekiah reading fails on chronology, since he was already ten or twelve years old when the words were spoken.
The Messiah; the Hezekiah reading fails because at his birth the house of David still had a flourishing reputation, whereas the prophecy requires a stump.
Not argued, but the state described is decisive: a trunk cut off at the root, the royal family reduced to the obscurity of Jesse.
Not argued; the interest is in the law of growth from a humble beginning, and in the word that may lie behind the title Nazarene.

debates.question: Should the gifts of the Spirit be distinguished one from another?

positions.view: Not the first pair: it is enough that they are the qualifications of a governor and a teacher, though counsel and might are distinct, and the closing fear is a fear of reverence.
They form an ordered sevenfold endowment with which the Lord consecrates and equips him.
They are more than the heroic gifts of the old judges: the king is to be David and Solomon in one.
Each qualifies Christ for a distinct part of his office, and the verse proves the trinity of Persons.

outliers.note: Notes that the Hebrew word for the branch here is the one some have supposed to lie behind the evangelist's statement that the Messiah should be called a Nazarene.
Measures the promised endowment against the old charismatic heroes, saying it is more than the daring that marked Jephthah and Samson, since the future king was to be a David and a Solomon at once.

themes: And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:
And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord;

3.pericope_label: And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the LORD... And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers that he shall draw his breath in the fear of the Lord, so that it is the air in which he lives, reporting the alternative that he shall find a sweet savour, and noting that the noun our version gives as understanding means primarily scent; he sets the coming judgment against the corrupt judges Isaiah had already portrayed, emends the object of the smiting so that a slight alteration gives smite the tyrant, which parallels the ungodly better than the earth does, and defends the repeated girdle against fastidious critics, since emphasis by iteration is quite in Isaiah's manner and the doubling may imply an upper and a lower girdle as the sign of complete equipment. Delitzsch renders the first clause that the fear of Jehovah is fragrance to him, and rejects two scholars who made the smelling a keen judicial insight, since the verb with this preposition will not carry it.

Gill makes the poor the poor in spirit, hungering after righteousness, and has the King adorned with righteousness and strengthened by it. Calvin takes the verb of the first clause actively, so that shrewd discernment is numbered among the gifts of the Spirit and Christ need not learn from what he hears or sees; he narrows the second verse openly, since the prophet points out the persons to whom the grace of Christ strictly belongs, those humbled by a conviction of their poverty, so that Christ is guardian not of all men whatsoever but of such as know themselves destitute of every good; and he reads the girdle as a royal emblem rather than a garment, supported from the passage where taking away the authority of kings is described as God ungirding them.

Clarke reports an emendation reading not the rod of his mouth but the blast of it, from a root meaning to blow, and calls it ingenious and probable, since the Greek and Chaldee rendering by the word of his mouth suits the correction better than the received text and blast makes an exact parallel to the breath of the lips; at the girdle he observes that all the ancient versions but one use two different words in the two halves of the line and concludes that the tautology arose from a transcriber's mistake. Wesley declines the figure of the first clause and reads a moral rule, that he shall not judge rashly or partially but considerately and justly, and makes the rod the word, the sceptre by whose preaching the world was subdued, drawing the point that Christ's kingdom is not of this world.

debates.question: What does the verb of smelling mean in the third verse?

positions.view: He shall draw his breath in the fear of the Lord, which is the air in which he lives; or possibly, he shall find a sweet savour in it.
The fear of Jehovah is fragrance to him — not, as two scholars would have it, a keen judicial insight into that fear.
Taken actively, a shrewd discernment numbered among the gifts of the Spirit, so that Christ need not learn from what he hears or sees.
No figure at all, but a moral rule: he shall not judge rashly or partially but considerately and justly, as the fear of God obliges every judge.
A discernment with an object, the power of telling who fears God from who does not.

debates.question: Is the repeated word for girdle a corruption?

positions.view: Yes: all the ancient versions but one use two different words, and the prophet would not have repeated one when an obvious synonym lay to hand, so the tautology arose from a transcriber's mistake.

No: the repetition has needlessly offended fastidious critics, since emphasis by iteration is quite in Isaiah's manner, and the doubling may imply an upper and a lower girdle as the sign of complete equipment.
The question does not arise, since what is meant is a royal emblem: to be girded is to be exalted to royal authority.
Not raised; the girdle is what adorns and strengthens him for the constant performance of righteousness.

outliers.note: Carries two conjectural emendations in three verses: the blast rather than the rod of his mouth, on the ground that it parallels the breath of the lips exactly; and the second girdle as a copyist's tautology.
Restricts the grace of the fourth verse explicitly, saying Christ is the guardian not of all men whatsoever but only of those who know themselves destitute of everything good.

themes: And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the Lord: and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears:

But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked.
And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins.

6.pericope_label: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid... for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea

schools.summary: Ellicott insists the animal world is genuinely included and finds it significant of the prophet's sympathy that he thinks of it as sharing in redemption, rapine and cruelty even there being marks to him of an imperfect order and the very instincts of the brute creation due to be changed; at the serpent's hole he identifies the creatures as the cobra and the great viper and measures the promise by present feeling, since the sight of a child beside such a hole would now make its mother scream with terror; and at the close he allows that the pronoun may refer back to the beasts, so that a restored Eden is in view, while noting that the words equally bear a general statement that none shall hurt or destroy. Delitzsch marks structure rather than substance, the righteous conduct of the Son of David having been described and now the peace prevailing under his government, extending even to the animal world and consequent on a knowledge of God become universal.

Gill reads the passage wholly of the Church: the cow and the bear feed together in one church state, the one having dispensed the milk of the divine word and the other worried the lambs of Christ, now of one nature and without fear; and he sets the fulfilment after the destruction of antichrist, when the saints will no longer be harassed by men like those creatures for cruelty or cunning. Calvin holds both senses together, the prophet ascending from the body to the head and descending again since Christ reigns not for himself but for those who believe, though the discourse looks beyond even that to a blessed restoration of the world, the order that obtained before man's apostasy; at the serpent he infers that men dread poison only because they do not deserve that God should place every part of the world under their control, and that since the creatures may injure even infants the whole race is stained with pollution from the womb; and at the close he declares plainly for men, who will have laid aside their natural depravity, meaning believers truly regenerated.

Clarke sets the passage beside its pagan parallels, the idea of a renewed golden age being much the same in oriental writers as in the Greek and Latin poets, and quotes a Roman eclogue in which the serpent's brood dies, the ground refuses noxious plants and the flocks no longer fear the great lions; at the serpent's den he reports a reading from the Targum and a Jewish commentator on which the phrase means the pupil of the serpent's eye, the child taking the glitter for crystal and putting out his hand to seize it. Wesley gives both senses at once, the creatures restored to the innocency they had before the fall and men of fierce disposition so transformed by grace as to become gentle, and locates the holy mountain in Zion, in the church.

debates.question: Is the peaceable kingdom about animals or about men?

positions.view: Wholly about men in the Church, the bear being the man who worried the lambs of Christ and is now of one nature with them.
Both at once: the creatures restored to their pre-fall innocency, and fierce men transformed by grace.
The animal world is genuinely included, since rapine and cruelty even there are marks of an imperfect order and the instincts of the brutes are to be changed.
The prophet moves between body and head, but the discourse looks beyond both to a restoration of the world's original order.
The question is not pressed; the passage describes the peace prevailing under the government already described, extending even to the animal world.
Not a den at all but the pupil of the serpent's eye, which sparkles in the mouth of the hole so that a child reaches for it as for crystal.
A real hole, and the creatures are the cobra and the great viper, so that the promise is measured by a mother's present terror at the sight.
The danger is the point, not the den: that creatures may injure even infants shows the whole race stained from the womb.
The child plays there without fear or danger, and that is all the verse says.

outliers.note: Sets the prophecy beside the classical golden age, quoting a Roman eclogue on the dying of the serpent's brood, ground that refuses noxious plants, and flocks that no longer fear the lions.

Turns the danger of serpents into an argument about inherited guilt: men fear poison only because they do not deserve dominion over the world, and the creatures' power to injure infants shows the race polluted from the womb.

themes: The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.
And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.
And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’ den.
They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea.

10.pericope_label: And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people... and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth

schools.summary: Ellicott ties the root back to the chapter's opening and pictures the new shoot of the fallen tree growing like a stately palm on the heights, a signal round which distant nations might rally, noting that the title is applied to the glorified Christ in the Revelation and that the verb for seeking implies the particular seeking of wisdom and illumination; he takes the first deliverance implied in the second to be obviously the Exodus, and finds in the twelfth verse a detail the versions lose, that the outcasts are masculine and the dispersed feminine, so that both sexes alike share in the restoration. Delitzsch frames the rest of the chapter as a series of questions, the first being how a king can reign in the midst of a nation scattered far from its native land, and the next arising from the mention of Israel and Judah together, whether the rent in the nation's unity will continue.

Gill places the gathering in the ministration of the Gospel, where Christ is held forth as the only Saviour and the gathering continues until all his people are brought in. Calvin locates the difficulty rather than the date, since that the Gentiles who formerly abhorred the Jews should bow before their King seemed incredible and the promise was ridiculed for centuries, such a gathering being more naturally looked for while the kingdom flourished than after it was cut down; on the second recovery he gives the reason for the reminder, that recalling a past deliverance keeps the elect from doubting God is as able to deliver them now as their fathers found him in Egypt; and he reads the ensign two ways, either as terrifying the adversaries so they dare not prevent the return or as signalling to the exiles not to hesitate, before turning it into use, that as an ensign is lifted in an army so soldiers may assemble and each keep his place, so an ensign is held out to us, which is the gospel.

Clarke will allow no partial fulfilment, saying this part of the chapter contains a prophecy that certainly remains yet to be accomplished; he reports a manuscript variant giving the present participle, so that the root is said to stand and to have stood as an ensign, notes that many manuscripts read the divine name differently at the eleventh verse, and passes on a Jewish commentator's identification of the islands of the sea with the Roman and Turkish empires. Wesley reads the promised rest as the resting-place, the temple or church, whose glory will exceed the tabernacle's but be spiritual, and takes the first deliverance to be the return from Babylon, from which it follows that this second must belong to the days of the Messiah.

Henry finds a partial accomplishment already, the great things God did for Hezekiah serving as an ensign that invited neighbouring nations to enquire after the wonders done in the land, on which errand the king of Babylon's ambassadors came.

positions.view: In part already, under Hezekiah, whose deliverance drew the neighbouring nations to enquire.
Not yet at all: this part of the chapter contains a prophecy that certainly remains to be accomplished.
In the ministration of the Gospel, and continuing until all his people are gathered in from every part of the world.
The date matters less than the difficulty: that the Gentiles should bow before this King was ridiculed for centuries, precisely because the kingdom had been cut down.
The signal is the root of Jesse itself, a stately growth seen from afar round which the nations rally.

debates.question: What is the first deliverance that the second recovery is measured against?

positions.view: The Exodus, obviously: from extremest misery they then entered on their life as a nation, and that is to be reproduced yet more wonderfully.
Egypt, and the reminder exists so the elect may not doubt that God can deliver now as their fathers found him able then.
The return from Babylon, from which it follows that this second recovery belongs to the days of the Messiah.
Not decided; the interest is in the text of the verse and in the identity of the islands of the sea.

outliers.note: Recovers a distinction the versions lose at the twelfth verse, that the outcasts are grammatically masculine and the dispersed feminine, and reads it as implying that both sexes alike share in the restoration.
Passes on a Jewish commentator's identification of the islands of the sea with the Roman and Turkish empires.

themes: And in that day there shall be a root of Jesse, which shall stand for an ensign of the people; to it shall the Gentiles seek: and his rest shall be glorious.

And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.
And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.

13.pericope_label: The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off... And there shall be an highway for the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the healed division national: the prophet's vision would have been incomplete without unity, and looking back he saw almost from the first a deep cleavage between north and south widening century by century, which in the times of the Christ the sense of unity should outweigh, connecting the hope with Hezekiah's own efforts. He warns that our version of the fourteenth verse is ambiguous and half suggests the Philistines will carry the returning Israelites, the Greek going further still with their speeding on wings in the ships of the aliens, whereas what is meant is that the exiles swoop like a bird of prey upon the shoulder of the Philistines, that word describing the shape of the seaward-sloping country. He prefers bay or gulf to tongue, identifies it as the Gulf of Suez, and grants that the river is the word commonly used of the Euphrates while preferring the Nile from the parallelism; and he describes the highway as the raised embanked road Eastern kings built for the march of armies. Delitzsch treats the fourteenth verse as the next of his questions, whether the warlike Philistines, the predatory nomads of the east, the unbrotherly Edomites, the boasting Moabites and the cruel Ammonites will weaken the new Israel as they did the old.

Gill widens the healed division as far as it will go, taking in whatever envy has subsisted between Jew and Gentile and then whatever has appeared in one Christian church or denomination against another, all to cease when the Gospel takes hold in its power and purity; he reports two Jewish commentators for reading the river as the Nile, and takes the highway into his own scheme of prophecy, holding that when the Mahometan, Pagan and Papal kingdoms are destroyed with their several religions the way of truth will lie open to the remnant. Calvin widens it to religion, dwelling on the allaying of domestic quarrels so that the children of Abraham may cease to harass one another and unite in the same worship; he explains the tongue of the sea by the resemblance of a bay to a man putting out his tongue, and makes a general point about expectation at the highway, that the people would perceive in the deliverance from Babylon the same power they had seen in the deliverance from Egypt, so that what the Lord has once performed we may look for again.

Clarke works on the verbs of the fifteenth verse, reporting that the Chaldee gives a word meaning shall desolate and that the Greek, Latin and Chaldee read a form meaning shall make it passable, supplying a pronoun the sense requires though no manuscript confirms it. Wesley reports that geographers give the name tongue to promontories shooting into the sea, takes the river for the Nile, and adds that the seven streams are what it is famous for.

debates.question: How far does the healing of the old division extend?

positions.view: To the nation only: the cleavage between north and south, which the sense of unity should at last outweigh.
To religion: the children of Abraham ceasing to harass one another and uniting in the same worship.
To the whole Church: envy between Jew and Gentile, and then between one Christian denomination and another, all ceasing together.
Not to everyone: the adversaries cut off are the few who continue in enmity, the body of Ephraim being supposed reconciled.
The question is whether the surrounding nations will weaken the new Israel as they did the old.

debates.question: Is the river of the fifteenth verse the Euphrates or the Nile?

positions.view: The word is the one commonly used of the Euphrates and most commentators take it so, but elsewhere it stands in parallel with the sea of Egypt and there means the Nile, which may well be accepted here.
The Nile, which waters the whole of Egypt and divides it into many parts.
The Nile, whose seven streams are what it is famous for in all authors.
Two Jewish commentators read the Nile; the destroying is the drying up, in allusion to the Red Sea.
The question of identity is left aside for the verbs, which the ancient versions render as desolating and as making passable.

outliers.note: Reads the highway of the last verse through his own scheme of prophecy, in which the Mahometan, Pagan and Papal kingdoms are destroyed with their religions before the way of truth lies open to the remnant.

Reports that the Greek version turned the flight upon the Philistines' shoulder into the Israelites speeding on wings in the ships of the aliens, against the sense he defends, of exiles swooping like a bird of prey on the seaward slope the word describes.

themes: The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.

But they shall fly upon the shoulders of the Philistines toward the west; they shall spoil them of the east together: they shall lay their hand upon Edom and Moab; and the children of Ammon shall obey them.

And the Lord shall utterly destroy the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and with his mighty wind shall he shake his hand over the river, and shall smite it in the seven streams, and make men go over dryshod.
And there shall be an highway for the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria; like as it was to Israel in the day that he came up out of the land of Egypt.
